title_en: The Ethics Problem in Financial Services (Dr. Moira Somers & Philippa Hann) | #425
title_zh: 金融服务业的伦理难题（Dr. Moira Somers 与 Philippa Hann）| #425
subtitle_zh: 两位作者解析为何好人会用别人的钱做坏事，以及如何守护自己的"伦理健康"。
summary_zh: 本期 The Rational Reminder（第 425 期）由 PWL Capital 的 Benjamin Felix 与 Cameron Passmore 主持，嘉宾是新书 The Fault Lines of Finance 的两位合著者：临床神经心理学家 Dr. Moira Somers，以及执业二十年、专攻金融服务诉讼、现任英国财务规划公司 Paradigm Norton 首席执行官的律师 Philippa Hann。节目的核心论点是：金融不当行为（financial misconduct）通常并非由精神变态者犯下，而是好人在压力、诱惑与糟糕的系统里一步步"伦理漂移"的结果。两位作者给出几条关键论据：其一，Association of Certified Fraud Examiners 的报告连续十余年把"财务问题"列为头号危险信号，而金融行业又天然提供了接触他人钱财的机会；其二，伦理是一项"团队运动"，系统与文化至关重要，新人、被孤立的员工和新任管理者尤其脆弱；其三，她们设计了可自己走一遍的十二步"道德操作系统"（moral operating system），并强调自尊（self-esteem）与自我关怀（self-compassion）；其四，从行为伦理学（behavioral ethics）角度看，理解自己的脆弱点比分辨对错更能左右行为，监管者、保险机制与普通投资者也都各有可为。本集为从业者与投资者提供了一份照看"伦理健康"、识别风险的实用指南。

turns.en: So we have this concept in the book of other people's money because it's really important when you are working in finance that you remember. It's not your money. So it's doing bad things with other people's money whether that's trying to take it for yourself or guiding or advising somebody to direct their money in a way
turns.zh: 所以我们在书里有一个概念叫"别人的钱"（other people's money），因为当你从事金融行业时，很重要的一点是要记住：那不是你的钱。所以就是用别人的钱去做坏事——无论是想把它据为己有，还是引导或建议某人把钱投向某种

turns.en: which is just not in their best interests. And what motivated each of you to write a book about financial misconduct? I spent 20 years suing financial advice as wealth managers and banks. In doing that, I kept asking myself, you know, when you're looking on the inside of somebody else's inbox,
turns.zh: 并不符合他最佳利益的方向。那么，是什么促使你们各自写了一本关于金融不当行为的书呢？我花了二十年时间起诉理财顾问、财富管理机构和银行。在做这件事的过程中，我一直在问自己：你知道，当你在翻看别人的收件箱内部时——

turns.en: which is what you do during the disclosure process and you're reading all the threads, you're seeing the decisions in real time, if you like, the memos, the transcripts of conversations, the emails that are going on, you've got your client giving you their witness statement when you get to court,
turns.zh: 那正是你在证据披露（disclosure）过程中做的事——你读着所有的邮件往来，几乎是实时地看到那些决策、那些备忘录、那些谈话记录、那些来来往往的邮件；到了法庭上，你的委托人给你他们的证人陈述，

turns.zh: 对方也在提供证据。你见过那份证人陈述。在我二十几岁、刚入行的头几年，我负责打理那些大型诉讼案件，那时候我很容易把人按一种迪士尼式的方式归类——你知道，这些人是好人，那些人是坏人。

turns.en: So I always happen to be acting for the good guys and gives the bad guys. It's not that simple. And so as I went through my career, I just kept seeing the same things. I kept having conversations with people on the other side of a courtroom or the other side of a mediation room and I mean, I met some psychopaths,
turns.zh: 所以我碰巧总是在替好人打官司、对付坏人。但事情没那么简单。随着我职业生涯的推进，我一直在看到同样的情形。我一直和法庭对面、或调解室对面的人交谈。我是说，我确实碰到过一些精神变态者，

turns.en: but largely they were not psychopaths. And I just had this niggling question of why did it happen? There was an easier option. turns.zh: 但绝大多数情况下他们并不是精神变态者。我心里一直有个挥之不去的疑问：这到底是怎么发生的？明明有更简单的选项，明明有一件显然该做的事，他们却没有去做。我想弄明白为什么。但当你是一名律师时，没有人会花钱请你去问这类问题。

turns.en: So I had to wait until I stopped being a lawyer. When I stopped being a lawyer, I just had this desire to answer that question. Why did good people do bad things with other people's money? turns.zh: 所以我不得不等到自己不再做律师之后。当我不再做律师时，我就特别想回答那个问题：为什么好人会用别人的钱去做坏事？而且我自己也曾待在一家律所的顶层。我是股权合伙人（equity partner），在董事会里，在执行委员会里。

turns.en: I was running a large division of 120 lawyers. I had several tens of million pounds that I was responsible for. And I felt the pressures. turns.zh: 我管理着一个有 120 名律师的大部门。我手上有几千万英镑的责任。我感受过那种压力。我体会过带进一个了不起的新客户所带来的价值感，体会过开出一张大账单时受到的追捧。我也体会过那种羞耻、恐惧和难过——

turns.en: of being not the top of the pile. And so really, the desire to write the book was trying to understand why it happens and trying to save myself from being one of those people. turns.zh: 那种没能待在金字塔尖的感觉。所以老实说，我想写这本书，是想弄明白这种事为什么会发生，也是想把自己从"变成那种人"里救出来。我在一次会议上见到了 Moira，我不知道当时有没有别人看到我头顶亮起的那盏灯泡——就在她发言的时候，我对自己说：

turns.en: that's the lady I need to come and help you write this. Wow. Moira. For both of us, there was both a prevention and a promotion aspect or aspirations for the book. turns.zh: 这就是我需要请来帮我一起写这本书的那位女士。哇。Moira。对我们两个人来说，这本书都既有"预防"的一面，也有"倡导"的一面，或者说抱负。当然，我想做点能够预防我所目睹的那些伤害的事，而不是总是被人叫去收拾残局、

turns.en: because I'm often called in sometimes by regulators, sometimes by insurers, sometimes just by families to deal with the fallout of the fraud or the financial abuse or whatever it's been. turns.zh: 你会去接触那些被欺诈、或沦为金融不当行为受害者的家庭，因为我们一直以来跟你合作，面对的都是那些很有钱、正试图弄清楚怎样用钱尽可能改善自己生活的人。

turns.en: But of course, it makes sense that you would have to deal with situations, I guess, the opposite end of that spectrum. Sometimes it's not the opposite end. turns.zh: 但当然，这也说得通——我想你得去处理那种光谱另一端的情形。有时候并不是另一端。有钱人是那些想算计他们的人绝佳的猎物。这些年来我们聊过多少次"钱的心理学"啊，

turns.en: that it brings out so much emotion and so another actual definition, I guess, of financial misconduct is using your own personal power to control people financially. Even if it's with sort of their consent, using money as an instrument of control, it might not be professional misconduct but it is kind of personal misconduct
turns.zh: 它能引出那么多的情绪。所以金融不当行为还有另一个实际定义，我猜，就是利用你个人的权力去在财务上控制别人。即便对方算是同意了，把钱当成一种控制的工具——它也许算不上职业不当行为，但确实是一种个人层面的不当行为，

turns.en: within the family sphere, for example, or the friendship sphere. So that too becomes something that it's necessary to unpack when we think about what leads people to do unethical things. I do want to talk about that because the way you guys approach it, I think, is just fascinating. But before we go there, can you talk
turns.zh: 发生在家庭圈子里，比方说，或者朋友圈子里。所以这也成了我们在思考"是什么驱使人们做出不合伦理的事"时，必须去拆解的东西。我确实想聊这个，因为我觉得你们俩切入的角度实在迷人。但在往那儿走之前，你们能不能先谈谈，

We went back and had a look at all the reports from the Association of Certified Fraud Examiner's. And the number one red flag for the last, I think, 14 years,
turns.zh: 为什么偏偏是金融服务业看起来特别容易滋生金融不当行为？我们来谈谈那种主要导致职业不当行为的情形。我们回过头去查了 Association of Certified Fraud Examiners（注册舞弊审查师协会）的所有报告。在过去大约 14 年里——

turns.en: which is the entire collection of the global report of all the fraud investigators who have looked at people doing bad things with money and that is financial problems. turns.zh: 也就是那份全球报告的全部收录范围，那些调查过"人们用钱做坏事"的舞弊调查员们得出的头号危险信号（red flag），就是财务问题（financial problems）。财务问题是最大的隐患。所以我们把它放进第一个盒子里：如果你管不住自己的财务，如果你入不敷出，如果你背着债，

turns.en: then you are one of the most highly likely people to be involved in some sort of financial misconduct. Add into that the fact that the financial services industry gives you access to influencing people with their money. So it provides the opportunities that being a doctor doesn't, for example, or even being a lawyer doesn't.
turns.zh: 那么你就是最有可能卷入某种金融不当行为的那类人之一。再叠加一个事实：金融服务业给了你影响他人钱财的门路。所以它提供了那种当医生、甚至当律师都没有的机会。

turns.en: You don't really touch other people's money. You add those two things in together. Then the third one is you are working with money. You are in a world where people don't go to financial plans when they don't have money. They go when they have money. It's a potential way to earn a lot of money and potentially attracts people
turns.zh: 你其实碰不到别人的钱。你把这两件事加在一起。第三点是，你在跟钱打交道。你所处的这个世界里，人们不会在自己没钱的时候去找理财规划师，而是在有钱的时候才去。这是一条潜在的赚大钱的路子，因而也可能吸引那些

turns.en: that think that earning a lot of money is important. And then being thrown into a world where lots of people have lots of wealth and then that feels very normal and it feels like something you should have and it feels like something you want. You also throw into that the fact that we're not as rational as we think we are.
turns.zh: 认为赚大钱很重要的人。然后被扔进一个很多人很有钱的世界，那种感觉就变得非常"正常"，感觉那是你本该拥有的东西，是你想要的东西。你还要再加上一个事实：我们并没有自己以为的那么理性。

turns.en: So it's a whole big recipe of things that means that the financial services industry unfortunately is an area where that financial misconduct is more likely to happen because you have all of those elements of it. Sounds like trust and opportunity really kind of boils down to people
turns.zh: 所以这是一整份由诸多要素调出来的"配方"，意味着金融服务业不幸地成了一个更容易发生金融不当行为的领域，因为你把这些要素全占齐了。听起来，信任和机会说到底就是：人们

turns.en: tend to trust people who are in a financial services type role and then there's an opportunity because you're close to the money. Well, also there's that information inequality as well. It's a bit like that white coat. You know, I don't go into a garage and argue with the mechanic. I say, well, if you say I need a widget, I believe you.
turns.zh: 倾向于信任那种担任金融服务类角色的人，然后又有机可乘，因为你离钱很近。嗯，还有那种信息不对等。这有点像那件白大褂。你知道，我走进一家修车厂，是不会跟机修工争辩的。我会说，嗯，既然你说我需要一个什么零件，我就信你。

The more emotion that people have around a topic and heaven knows that money evokes emotion, the more likely it is that you will get extreme responses of either huge difficulty trusting
turns.zh: 因为我对此懂得不够多。而且我相信你在那里是为了帮我。所以这是非常相似的一件事。人们围绕一个话题投入的情绪越多——天知道钱能勾起多少情绪——你就越可能得到极端的反应：要么极度难以信任，

turns.en: in which case you probably will never see those people or it will take a very, very long courtship to get involved with them or they come in and they just sort of say, here, kind of like you do a doctor. I've got all this. I don't know what to do with it. Can you just tell me what to do with it?
turns.zh: 那种情况下你多半永远见不到这些人，或者要花很长很长的"追求期"才能跟他们搭上关系；要么他们进来就干脆地说，喏，就像你对医生那样——我这儿有一大笔钱，我不知道该怎么办，你能不能直接告诉我该怎么处理？

turns.en: There's lots of evidence that the critical aspects of their brain actually go offline. They look very much when you put them in neuroimaging like the brains of people in prayer. turns.zh: 有大量证据表明，他们大脑中那些负责批判的部分其实会"下线"（go offline）。当你把他们放进神经影像（neuroimaging）设备里，他们的脑子看上去非常像那些正在祈祷的人的脑子。那些在接受理财建议时的人，其大脑状态和正在祈祷的人非常相像。他们感到安全，感到被信任。

turns.en: They feel open. Like I've got my hands out. Like I'm just ready to receive what it is you have to tell me. turns.en: when they're in that conversation with an expert. I definitely was experienced that with my clients. turns.zh: Eugene Soltes 是一位我挺喜欢追随的作者。他写了一本书叫 Why They Do It（《他们为什么这么做》）。它本质上是一本关于白领犯罪（white collar crimes）的揭秘之作。他发现，这些人并不是那种坐下来列一张利弊清单、

turns.en: Most of these people, it was an impulse. It was a momentary decision to just do the thing, to hide, to lie on the income statement that they had to give to the chair of the board. It wasn't well thought out. It was poor impulse control because they were tired. They were pressured. Everybody wanted a piece of them
turns.zh: 然后煞费苦心地算出"我干这事到底值不值"的人。对这些人中的大多数来说，那是一时的冲动。那是一个转瞬之间的决定：就做了那件事，去掩盖，在必须交给董事会主席的那份损益表上撒个谎。它并没有经过深思熟虑。它是糟糕的冲动控制，因为他们累了，他们承受着压力，人人都想从他们身上分一杯羹，

turns.en: and they maybe didn't know what to do. And so that mapping out of what would I do in these circumstances? How do I prevent myself from getting in these circumstances? And who are my people? Who are the people that I can pick up the phone and call when I am struggling with an issue? And I don't know what the right thing to do is
turns.zh: 而他们也许不知道该怎么做。所以，把"这些情形下我会怎么做？我该如何防止自己陷入这些情形？谁是我的人（my people）？"梳理清楚——就是那些当我为一个问题苦恼、不知道该怎么做才对时，我可以拿起电话就打过去的人，

turns.en: or even worse, when I do know what the right thing to do is, but I don't want to do it because it's going to be hard. So identifying who are your people that will solidly stand behind you as you do the right thing. You tell the story of Tom Hardin in the book, who we had on this podcast in episode 398. You talked with us in the book too
turns.zh: 或者更糟，当我明明知道该怎么做、却因为太难而不想去做时。所以，识别出谁是你的人、谁会坚定地站在你身后支持你做正确的事。你们在书里讲了 Tom Hardin 的故事，他上过我们这档播客的第 398 期。你们在书里也跟我们聊到

turns.en: about how he did call people, but he kind of used it as... He used it for confirmation bias is what he used it for. Yeah. When psychology, one of our ethical guidelines is if you're concerned about somebody else's conduct, the conduct of a colleague, you have to reach out to that colleague directly. Oh, that's hard. That's really hard.
turns.zh: 他确实给人打了电话，但他有点把它当成……他其实是拿它来做确认偏误（confirmation bias）的，对吧。是的。在心理学界，我们的一条伦理准则是：如果你担心某个人——某位同事——的行为，你必须直接去找那位同事。哦，这很难。这真的很难。

turns.en: The notion is that you've got to strengthen yourself to have hard conversations. I uncovered misconduct in one of the family offices that I'm working with. This just happened a couple of months ago. It was obvious that somebody that everybody loved was going to have to be let go. And I had to call it Philippa and say,
turns.zh: 这个理念是，你得让自己强大起来，去进行那些艰难的对话。我在自己合作的一家家族办公室（family office）里揭发了一起不当行为。这事就发生在几个月前。显然，一个所有人都喜欢的人将不得不被辞退。我得给 Philippa 打电话，说：

turns.en: Oh my God, I hate this. I hate this. This wasn't a psychopathic person. This wasn't a narcissistic person. This was somebody who was trying to do the right thing and went horribly wrong. I had called up Jim Grubman and Philippa and say, help me see what I'm not seeing or help me conceptualize this in a way
turns.zh: 天哪，我讨厌这件事，我讨厌这件事。这个人不是精神变态者，也不是自恋者。这是一个想做正确的事、结果却出了大岔子的人。我给 Jim Grubman 和 Philippa 都打了电话，说：帮我看看我漏掉了什么，或者帮我把这件事梳理清楚，

turns.en: so that when the rubber hits the road, I can do the right thing. And they were very helpful. And what a privilege to be that person for someone else. It is so much easier to see it if someone else than it is to see it for yourself. We sort of ended up sort of a bit aghast because this is the stuff we've been writing about
turns.zh: 好等到了关键时刻、真刀真枪的时候，我能做出正确的事。他们帮了大忙。而能成为别人的这样一个人，是何等的荣幸。看清别人身上的问题，总是比看清自己的要容易得多。我们最后有点惊呆了，因为这正是我们一直在书里写的东西，

turns.en: and it was happening to Moira. And so that was wild actually to see the book in action. That is very cool. We had Jim on, Jim Grubman on an episode 282. I think you mentioned ambition, Moira. And that's one of the things we talked to Tom Harden about is that his own desire to be successful was one of his big weak points
turns.zh: 而它却发生在了 Moira 身上。所以亲眼看到这本书"活"起来，其实挺不可思议的。这非常酷。我们请 Jim Grubman 上过第 282 期节目。我觉得你提到了野心，Moira。这正是我们跟 Tom Hardin 聊到的一点：他自己想出人头地的渴望，正是他最大的弱点之一，

turns.en: to let him to do what he did. Any one of the strengths that we have can be turned into a weakness. Are you confident? Whoops, watch out. Are you ambitious? Whoops. Are you not confident? Whoops. Are you very humble? Oh, just knowing yourself and knowing what to do, knowing how that could show up.
turns.zh: 把他引向了他所做的事。我们所拥有的任何一项长处，都可能被翻转成一个弱点。你自信吗？哎哟，小心。你有野心吗？哎哟。你不自信吗？哎哟。你非常谦逊吗？哦，就是要了解你自己、知道该怎么做，知道这些会如何显现出来。

turns.en: If you think of how would a spy approach you? What would Matt or Hari do to do it to you? What would an objective outsider say that your vulnerabilities are? How do you deal with those? And being isolated is one of those vulnerabilities. Having that sounding board outside of yourself and one of the real difficult places to be
turns.zh: 如果你想想，一个间谍会怎么接近你？Matt 或者 Hari 会怎么对你下手？一个客观的局外人会说你的脆弱点在哪里？你该如何应对它们？而被孤立正是这些脆弱点之一。在你自身之外拥有这样一个可以商量的人（sounding board），而真正艰难的处境之一，

turns.en: is either a new person in a firm which leaves you very isolated and wanting to please or managers, particularly new managers when they're suddenly moving. I mean, I remember moving into that management position and feeling like I had to have all the answers, feeling like I had to make all the decisions,
turns.zh: 要么是刚进一家公司的新人——这会让你非常孤立、非常想讨好别人——要么是管理者，特别是那些刚被提拔、突然走马上任的新任管理者。我是说，我记得自己走进那个管理岗位时，感觉必须掌握所有的答案，感觉必须做出所有的决定，

turns.en: feeling like I couldn't make a mistake, et cetera, et cetera. And those are particularly when you're feeling that way an incredibly vulnerable position. Is that resonating with you, Cameron? You sure is. It's so interesting. It's very much the system, right? And the rules inside the system can cause this issue to be exasperated.
turns.zh: 感觉自己不能犯错，等等等等。而这些恰恰是当你有那种感觉时，一个极其脆弱的处境。这在你身上有共鸣吗，Cameron？绝对有。太有意思了。这很大程度上是系统的问题，对吧？而系统内部的规则会让这个问题被放大。

turns.en: Are you run your firm? How you create an environment for integrity, for relationships is so important when you're running a financial firm? One of the cases that we highlight we sort of divide the book into three sections. So there's sort of what's been wrong with traditional ethics training and what needs to happen to make it better.
turns.zh: 你怎么经营你的公司？当你在经营一家金融公司时，你如何营造一个讲究诚信、讲究关系的环境，是如此重要。我们着重讲的一个案例——我们大体上把这本书分成了三个部分。所以有一部分讲的是传统伦理培训哪里出了问题，以及需要怎样做才能让它更好。

turns.en: What do the regulators want us to know? What does the evidence, the research evidence say? That's the first part of the book. And then the second part of the book is case studies. Study after study of some of the headlines they hit the news, some of the cases that Philip was involved in,
turns.zh: 监管机构希望我们知道什么？研究证据、也就是那些实证研究又说了什么？这是书的第一部分。然后书的第二部分是案例研究。一个接一个的案例，有些是登上过新闻头条的，有些是 Philippa 参与过的案子，

turns.en: some of the cases that I was involved with as a psychologist. Just looking at what was there in the firm that allowed things to go on, in some cases that encouraged bad stuff to go on or that didn't prevent it. Like having somebody that you trust implicitly as your accountant and you don't require a second signature.
turns.zh: 有些是我作为一名心理学家参与过的案子。就是去看，公司里究竟有些什么，让这些事情得以持续下去；在某些案例里，甚至鼓励坏事发生，或者没能阻止它。比如说，有那么一个你完全信任、让他当你的会计师的人，而你并不要求第二个签名。

turns.en: Well, that's just setting somebody up. If things start going awry in their life, you've just set them up to engage in workplace embezzlement
turns.zh: 嗯，那其实就是在给某人"下套"。如果他们的生活开始出岔子，你就等于把他们推向了职场侵占（workplace embezzlement），

turns.en: that can go undetected. Yes, it is his fault or her fault, but it's kind of also your fault if you're the business owner and haven't set up better practices. We have to think about the fact that we're working with vulnerable human beings with all of these strengths and weaknesses and that systems have a huge role to play
turns.zh: 而且可以不被察觉。是的，这是他的错或她的错，但如果你是那个企业主、却没有建立起更好的做法，那这在某种程度上也是你的错。我们必须考虑到这样一个事实：我们在跟脆弱的人打交道，他们带着所有这些长处和弱点，而系统扮演着极其重要的角色，

turns.en: and culture has a huge role to play and whether stuff is ethical or not. Even how easy do you make it to surface a mistake? I was just going to jump on that word culture because as you know in our environment, mistakes happen in trading, right? And the team knows it's never a bad time to make the right decision. And often you could say,
turns.zh: 文化也扮演着极其重要的角色，关乎一件事情到底合不合伦理。甚至——你让一个错误有多容易被浮出水面？我正想接过"文化"这个词，因为你知道，在我们的环境里，交易中是会出错的，对吧？而团队都知道，做正确的决定永远没有"太晚"这一说。你常常可以说，

turns.en: oh, the client would never notice, but everyone here knows, no, take the high road, always do what's right. You know what's right, do what's right. And it's just part of our culture, I believe, right, Ben? Yes, and part of our systems, like we're not punishing people for bringing forward a mistake like that,
turns.zh: 哦，客户永远不会发现的，但这里每个人都清楚：不，要走正道，永远做对的事。你知道什么是对的，就去做对的。而我相信，这只是我们文化的一部分，对吧，Ben？是的，也是我们系统的一部分，比如说我们不会因为有人把这样一个错误提出来就惩罚他，

turns.en: which I think is how you could get to a place where they would want to hide it. Yes, the system will pay for the mistake, not the person. But there's punishment and punishment. So there's punishment of telling someone off or saying, you will pay for it and all the rest of it. But there's also punishment in a sigh.
turns.zh: 我觉得这正是能让你走向那种"人们愿意把错误藏起来"的地方的关键。是的，是系统为这个错误买单，而不是那个人。但惩罚也分很多种。有的是把某人训斥一顿、或者说"你会为此付出代价"诸如此类的惩罚。但还有一种惩罚藏在一声叹气里。

turns.en: There's punishment in a look. All of that stuff, we are sucking in this information all the time. But one of the red flags that you should be looking out for is if people are not making mistakes. Anyone who doesn't make mistakes, I only ask a question to them. What's going on here? Because it's not normal to not make mistakes.
turns.zh: 还有一种惩罚藏在一个眼神里。所有这些东西，我们无时无刻不在吸收着。但你该留意的危险信号之一是：如果人们不犯错。任何一个不犯错的人，我只会问他们一个问题：这里到底发生了什么？因为不犯错是不正常的。

turns.en: Yeah, that's interesting. Mara, something that you mentioned a couple of times now that jumped out to me, the way that I read through the book was, it's often just regular, nice people who are doing bad stuff. But you mentioned psychopaths a couple of times. How worried should people in everyday life for doing consuming financial services
turns.zh: 是啊，这很有意思。Moira，有一件你已经提到好几次、让我印象特别深的事：我通读这本书时的感受是，往往就是普普通通的好人在做坏事。但你几次提到了精神变态者。在日常生活中，那些使用金融服务的人，

turns.en: be about psychopaths? The evidence is that they disproportionately gravitate towards financial services and business. To where the money is. Because that's where the money is. It's like the old story of the bad bank robber getting caught and it was asked, why do you keep robbing banks? And his answer was, well, that's where the money is.
turns.zh: 应该对精神变态者有多担心？证据表明，他们不成比例地被金融服务业和商业所吸引。被钱所在的地方吸引。因为那就是钱所在的地方。这就像那个老掉牙的故事：一个笨贼银行劫匪被抓了，别人问他，你为什么老抢银行？他的回答是，嗯，因为钱在那儿。

turns.en: So that's where the money is now. And we know that financial services are one of the top two targets for workplace fraud and financial misconduct. Because that's where the money is. And so pure psychopaths often aren't very successful. But sort of psychopath-light, the snakes and suits, there's a book that's been written by a Canadian,
turns.zh: 所以现在，钱就在那儿。而我们知道，金融服务业是职场舞弊和金融不当行为的头号或次号目标之一。因为那就是钱所在的地方。所以纯粹的精神变态者往往并不怎么成功。但那种"轻度精神变态"、那些"西装革履的毒蛇"（snakes in suits）——有一本书就是这么写的，作者是一位加拿大人，

turns.en: one of the world experts on psychopathy is actually here in Canada, Robert Hare. And he talks about, what does it look like when you're successful at this? And you tend to be charming. You know how to find people's longings and tap into them. You know how to court friendship with the right people. You rope them in, you seduce them
turns.zh: 世界上最顶尖的精神变态研究专家之一其实就在加拿大这里，Robert Hare。他谈到，当你在这条路上"成功"时，那是什么样子？你往往会很有魅力。你知道怎么找到人们内心的渴望并加以利用。你知道怎么跟对的人攀上交情。你把他们拉进来，你引诱他们，

turns.en: or you belittle them if you need to. It is a big issue. And they are the ones that tend to leave this trail of destruction then. If they're really, got really big brains, they often try to mastermind equally big schemes to get people out of the money, but boy, relationally and from a mental health perspective, they wreak havoc.
turns.zh: 或者在需要时贬低他们。这是个大问题。而且他们正是那种会留下一路破坏的人。如果他们脑子真的很好使，他们往往会精心策划同样庞大的骗局去掏空别人的钱，但天哪，从人际关系和心理健康的角度看，他们制造的是彻底的浩劫。

turns.en: And we were discussing this the other day, Moira and I. Because people are generally so relieved when the psychopath is no longer in the firm because they are so destructive, they tend to button down the hatches, breathe a sigh of relief, provide a reference to say, well, they worked between this date and that date and they turned up.
turns.zh: 我和 Moira 前几天还在讨论这个。因为当一个精神变态者终于不在公司里了，人们通常会松一大口气，因为他们太有破坏性了；大家往往会赶紧关上舱门，长舒一口气，然后提供一份推荐信，说，嗯，他们在这段时间到那段时间在这里工作过，而且他们有来上班。

turns.en: Actually, we're all a bit afraid to say, and I think they're a bit of a psychopath and I definitely wouldn't employ them because we're afraid of being sued. And it is a particular problem because you will see that they will move from firm to firm until they find the opportunity or they'll get away with staff
turns.zh: 其实，我们都有点不敢说"我觉得他有点像个精神变态者，我绝对不会雇他"，因为我们怕被起诉。而这确实是个特别的问题，因为你会看到他们从一家公司跳到另一家公司，直到找到那个机会；或者他们会带着一批人一起走，

turns.en: and they'll get away with staff and they'll take their yes people with them. And they will sink to wherever they can actually get away with whatever it is that they want to do that provides them with that, they get out of it, what they want to get out of it. And it is a real problem because non-psychopaths are just so relieved
turns.zh: 带着一批人一起走，还会带上那些唯命是从的人（yes people）。他们会沉到任何一个他们真能得逞的地方，去做他们想做的事、拿到他们想从里面拿到的东西。而这确实是个真问题，因为那些不是精神变态者的人

turns.en: to have them out of their lives that they walk away and it's understandable. Yeah, I think you referenced the paper, I think it's called the market from up financial misconduct, is that what it's called? The market work. Yeah, that's right. Advisors gravitate to certain firms after having conducted misconduct and then they end up.
turns.zh: 只要能把他们从自己的生活里赶走就大大松了口气，于是就一走了之——这可以理解。是啊，我想你引用了那篇论文，我记得它叫"金融不当行为的市场"（the market for financial misconduct），是这个名字吧？那篇市场的文章。对，没错。顾问在犯下不当行为之后会向某些公司聚集，然后他们最终……

turns.en: They are recruited. It's not just they gravitate towards it. They are recruited preferentially by certain firms who like to engage in exploitation of vulnerable people. How do we become ethical people? That's such a nice question after all this. That's an easy question, obvious one. I have a theory around
turns.zh: 他们是被招募的。这不只是他们自己往那边聚集。他们是被某些公司优先招募的，那些公司就喜欢从事对弱势群体的剥削。那我们怎样才能成为有道德的人？在聊了这么多之后，这真是个美好的问题。这是个简单的、显而易见的问题。我有一个理论：

turns.en: you look after your physical health, you look after your mental health. And I think there is an argument to say, and that's what we conclude in the book. You need to be taking steps to look after your ethical health. Spending some time working on yourself is vital for you to be able to look after your ethical health.
turns.zh: 你照看自己的身体健康，你照看自己的心理健康。我认为有一点是站得住脚的，也是我们在这本书里的结论：你需要采取一些步骤来照看自己的"伦理健康"（ethical health）。花些时间在自己身上下工夫，对于你能否照好自己的伦理健康至关重要。

turns.en: And there is this kind of triumvirates if you like of weirdly self-esteem. Because if you have self-esteem, you can say, I don't want to do that. Thanks very much. I'm good. People who lack self-esteem tend to go along to get along. So developing self-esteem and in order to develop self-esteem. So there was a research particular they did
turns.zh: 而且这里有那么一个"三位一体"（triumvirate），说来奇怪，头一个就是自尊（self-esteem）。因为如果你有自尊，你就能说，"我不想做那件事，谢谢，我很好。"而缺乏自尊的人往往会随大流、以求相安无事。所以要培养自尊。而为了培养自尊——有一项研究特别做过，

turns.en: with some school kids. They realized that kids who have high self-esteem have great exam results or have better exam results. So they went into schools and they bolstered up these kids and they gave them all this really huge self-esteem and they went into their exams and they did no better than anyone else.
turns.zh: 对象是一些学龄孩子。他们发现，那些自尊高的孩子考试成绩很好，或者说考得更好。于是他们走进学校，去给这些孩子打气，给他们灌上满满一大份自尊，然后让他们去考试——结果他们并不比任何人考得好。

turns.en: And what they realized as a result was that you don't get good exam results because you have good self-esteem. You have good self-esteem because you've put the work in to have the exam results. So in order to get good self-esteem, you have to put the work in. You need to go and do the exams. You need to go and make sure
turns.zh: 而他们由此意识到的是：你并不是因为自尊好才考得好，而是因为你下了功夫、考出了好成绩，才有了好的自尊。所以为了获得好的自尊，你必须下功夫。你得去把那些考试考出来。你得去确保

turns.en: that your private life is in good shape that you are tackling the difficult things that you're having the conversations that you're attempting those things. So self-esteem is really important. Self-compassion. It's really important, weirdly, that came out of our research. If you are able to say, well, it's okay that I made a mistake
turns.zh: 你的私人生活状态良好，你在啃那些难啃的事，你在进行那些该进行的对话，你在尝试那些该尝试的事。所以自尊真的很重要。还有自我关怀（self-compassion）。说来奇怪，这也是从我们的研究里冒出来的——它真的很重要。如果你能够说，嗯，我犯了个错，没关系，

turns.en: because I'm a human being and humans make mistakes. And it's okay to go and tell my boss, sorry, I think I made a mistake. Can you help me? And having enough compassion for yourself to say, can you help me? I mean, if someone goes to you as their boss and says, can you help me please? It's a totally different conversation.
turns.zh: 因为我是一个人，而人是会犯错的。而且，去跟我的老板说"对不起，我觉得我犯了个错，你能帮帮我吗"，这没关系。有足够的自我关怀去说出那句"你能帮帮我吗"——我是说，如果有人作为下属来找你这个老板，说"你能帮帮我吗"，那完全是一场不同的对话。

turns.en: In what circumstances are you ever going to say, no, I'm not going to help you? And that self-actualization piece through doing a work on yourself in terms of what are your values? What are your vulnerabilities? How are you going to deal with those? What are your non-negotiables? Do you understand yourself? Are you doing the journaling?
turns.zh: 在什么情况下你会说"不，我不帮你"？而那种通过在自身上下功夫达成的自我实现（self-actualization）——你的价值观是什么？你的脆弱点是什么？你打算如何应对它们？你那些不可谈判的底线是什么？你了解自己吗？你在写日记吗？

turns.en: Do you have your ethical sounding board around you? Do you know where to go and who to speak to? There is work which is involved in this. But that work, I promise you. Would you know this? It's so worth it. Nobody goes into a profession in order to wreak havoc. People go into a profession to help people and to achieve that sense of self.
turns.zh: 你身边有你的伦理"商量对象"（ethical sounding board）吗？你知道该去哪里、该找谁谈吗？这里面是需要下功夫的。但那份功夫，我向你保证——你知道吗？它太值得了。没有人入一行是为了去制造浩劫。人们入一行是为了帮助别人、为了获得那种自我价值感。

turns.en: And in order to avoid the pitfalls, you need to do that work on yourself. I love that answer. And I think even the willingness to do those things is perhaps seated in us way, way earlier. And I ask you, Cameron, how did you become ethical? When we ask that of the regulators, and I remember coming back and asking you this question,
turns.zh: 而为了避开那些陷阱，你需要在自己身上下这份功夫。我太喜欢这个答案了。我觉得，甚至那份"愿意去做这些事"的心，也许在我们身上扎得要早得多、早得多。我想问你，Cameron，你是怎么成为一个有道德的人的？当我们向监管机构问这个问题时——我记得回过头来也问过你这个问题——

turns.en: most people, first of all, point to people in very early childhood. They talk about their parents, people who taught them from a very young age. They talk about coaches, being part of a religious tradition. There's a foundational element to that that says there is right and there is wrong. This is what to do.
turns.zh: 大多数人首先会指向很小的时候（early childhood）遇到的人。他们谈自己的父母，谈那些从很小就教导他们的人。他们谈教练，谈自己所属的某个宗教传统。这里面有一个根基性的元素，它告诉你什么是对、什么是错，该怎么做，

turns.en: And also, this is what will happen. If you don't do the right thing, that's part of the answer to how do we become ethical is that we are taught by people who have our best interest in heart. And we are also modeled. There's a common saying that values are caught rather than taught. And so we see people around us doing the things
turns.zh: 还有：如果你不做正确的事，会发生什么。这也是"我们如何变得有道德"这个问题的一部分答案——我们是被那些把我们最佳利益放在心上的人教导的。而且我们还会被"示范"。有句常话说，价值观是被"感染"（caught）的，而不是被"教导"（taught）的。所以我们看着周围的人做那些事、

turns.en: or not doing the things that they're counseling us to do. And we see how that work out. Can somebody like me do this kind of thing too? For good or for ill? I think then as we get older, we do start to get explicit teaching, especially if we are in a profession that has ethics requirements as part of ongoing certification or whatever.
turns.zh: 或者不做那些他们劝我们去做的事，我们看着那样做会有什么结果。像我这样的人，也能做这种事吗？无论好坏。我想，随着我们长大，我们确实开始接受明确的教学，尤其是当我们身处一个把伦理要求作为持续认证一部分的职业里时。

turns.en: We start learning ethical reasoning. We might be actually taught. This is what you do here versus there. This is how to even think ethically. These are some of the thinking skills that are required. Where we found that the ethics breaks down is that it doesn't sufficiently engage the heart. I hate to sort of do that dichotomy.
turns.zh: 我们开始学习伦理推理（ethical reasoning）。我们也许会被实打实地教：在这里你该这样做，在那里你该那样做；这才是如何去进行伦理思考；这些是所需的一些思维技能。而我们发现伦理"崩塌"的地方在于，它没有充分地触及内心。我不想搞那种二分法，

turns.en: But in other words, it doesn't teach us what to do when it's tough to do the right thing. It just says do the right thing. Oh, well, thanks. That was helpful. Don't cross boundaries. Oh, great. But what if I have or what if it feels like it is ethical to cross that boundary? What if it feels cold and callous and absolutely heartless
turns.zh: 但换句话说，它没有教我们：当做正确的事很难时，该怎么办。它只是说，做正确的事。哦，好嘛，谢谢，这真有帮助。别越界。哦，太好了。可如果我……或者，如果越过那条界线感觉反而是合伦理的呢？如果告诉客户"我做不了这件事"感觉冷酷、无情、

turns.en: to tell a client that I can't do this thing? Well, oh, oh. I'm either hooped or I'm helped because I've had training on what to do. And I know who I can talk to when it's really, really hard. It's not a solo sport. Not from the earliest days that we're on the earth. We're always getting inputs on what it means
turns.zh: 绝对铁石心肠呢？那么，哦哦，我要么完蛋了，要么得救了——因为我接受过"该怎么做"的培训，而且我知道在真的很难很难的时候，我可以找谁谈。这不是一项单打独斗的运动。从我们在世上的最早时候起，我们就一直在接收关于

turns.en: to be ethical, to be a good person. I really love that part of our book, actually. Ethics isn't just about identifying when there's a problem in knowing what to do. It's about having the moral character to actually do something. I think when we were looking at that, it just kind of hit me like a freight train
turns.zh: "何为有道德、何为好人"的输入。我其实特别喜欢我们书里的那一部分。伦理不只是识别出哪里出了问题、知道该怎么做。它还要有真正去付诸行动的道德品格（moral character）。我想当我们审视这一点时，它就像一列货运火车一样猛地击中了我：

turns.en: that it's so true, not just knowing what the right answer is, but having the character, the motivation, ability, desire to feel uncomfortable to do the right thing at the same time was such a big thing when we were writing that. One of the things that comes up in your case studies, how I'm hardened is a good example
turns.zh: 这太真实了——不只是知道正确答案是什么，而是有那种品格、那种动力、那种能力、那种甘愿忍受不适去做正确事的渴望——在我们写那部分时，这可是一件天大的事。你的案例研究里反复出现的一点，我觉得 Tom Hardin 就是个好例子：

turns.en: where when we had them on this podcast, he tells his whole back story and you can tell he's like, he's a good person, he's raised well. If you asked younger Tom, if you would do the things that he did, he would say, absolutely not, but then he did them. What causes that ethical drift in people over time? Or what can cause it?
turns.zh: 我们请他上这档播客时，他讲了他完整的过往，你能听出来他是个好人，家教很好。如果你去问年轻时的 Tom，他会不会做他后来做的那些事，他会说，绝对不会——可他还是做了。是什么造成了人们随时间的这种"伦理漂移"（ethical drift）？或者说，什么能造成它？

turns.en: If you talk to him, you will know some of the story, but that is kind of universal. He was in an extraordinarily high-pressure environment that did not tell people what right looks like here and what wrong looks like here and what to do if you are tempted to cross the line. There was no explicit ethical teaching
turns.zh: 如果你跟他谈，你会知道其中一部分故事，但那其实是相当普遍的。他身处一个压力极大的环境，那环境并没有告诉人们：在这里，"对"是什么样、"错"是什么样，以及当你被诱惑去越线时该怎么办。从公司高层往下，都没有明确的伦理教导。

turns.en: from the firm leaders on down. There weren't conversations. It was sort of an assumption, well, don't cross the line. He was what, 26 when he started? Maybe not for that particular firm, but right out of college, he went into the hedge fund world at the end. It's kind of known for its ruthlessness.
turns.zh: 也没有那些对话。它有点像一种默认的假设：嗯，别越线就行。他开始的时候多大？26 岁吧？也许不是在那家特定的公司，但大学一毕业，他就进了对冲基金的世界，而那个世界向来以冷酷无情著称。

turns.en: So if you don't have people explicitly saying this is what right looks like and these are where your temptations are going to lie. We had one of the people that we highlight. She was having dinner with the bushes and the Reagans, these big names in American politics when she wasn't even 30 yet. And it was just because of her job,
turns.zh: 所以，如果没有人明确地说"这就是对的样子，这些就是你会面临的诱惑所在"——我们着重讲的一位人物，她还不到 30 岁，就在跟布什家族和里根家族这些美国政坛的大人物共进晚餐。而这仅仅因为她的工作，

turns.en: it was all very heady and you start to have a sense of, this is what normal looks like. And she said the notion that, huh, they're 60. I'm less than half their age. Maybe I shouldn't be having private tickets in the sports boxes. Maybe that isn't normative. But again, there was nobody that she could talk to about feelings
turns.zh: 那一切都令人飘飘然，你就开始有了一种"这就是正常"的感觉。她说，那个念头是：喂，他们都六十岁了，我连他们一半年纪都不到，也许我不该拿着体育包厢的私人门票，也许那并不"正常"。但同样地，她身边没有一个可以倾诉的人，去说那些

turns.en: that were sort of embarrassed about sometimes. Like, what do I do with my envy? What do I do with the fact that I am feeling really judgy about how this billionaire and their kids just think that they're all that in a bag of chips and that they can just treat us like we're nothing. What do I do with those feelings?
turns.zh: 她有时觉得有点难为情的感受。比如：我该怎么处理我的嫉妒？我该怎么处理这样一个事实——我对某位亿万富翁及其子女那种"觉得自己了不起、可以拿我们当空气"的做派感到特别看不顺眼、特别爱评判？我该怎么处理这些感受？

turns.en: What do I do with the fact that I want to be part of that family? Where do we go with that? You can learn how to manage difficult emotions but the impulse to just swap them away like they're nuisance mosquitoes and that we shouldn't bother acknowledging is the very thing that leads us to act out of them at a weak point.
turns.zh: 我该怎么处理"我想成为那个家庭一员"的这种念头？这些我们该往哪儿放？你可以学会如何管理那些艰难的情绪，但那种想把它们像讨厌的蚊子一样一巴掌拍走、觉得我们不该去承认它们的冲动，恰恰就是在某个脆弱点上驱使我们把它们付诸行动的东西。

turns.en: So that's what Tom Harden did. He was surrounded by all of this. He wanted to help a friend. It was well-motivated in the moment. He wanted to help a friend who was in a great distress. And then he realized, oh my gosh, my friend is making crap loads of money. And I'm being all high and mighty and not acting on knowledge that I had.
turns.zh: 所以 Tom Hardin 就是这么做的。他被这一切包围着。他想帮一个朋友。在那一刻，动机是好的。他想帮一个正陷入极大痛苦的朋友。然后他意识到：天哪，我朋友正在赚大钱，而我还在这儿端着架子、清高地不去利用我手上掌握的信息。

turns.en: Well, that sucks. And so slowly this drift began and he did reach out to people but he didn't reach out by saying, I have a dilemma. This is both sides of it. He just talked to people who he says, you know, offhand. They were some of the good guys but he didn't give them the whole fact case. They just said, oh, yeah, you're fine.
turns.zh: 嗯，那太糟糕了。于是这种"漂移"就慢慢开始了。他确实向人伸了手，但他伸手的方式并不是说"我有一个两难困境，这是它的两面"。他只是跟一些人随口聊了聊——他说，你知道，那些人里有些还是"好人"——但他没有把完整的事实摆给他们。他们只是说，哦，是啊，你没问题。

turns.en: So we talked to people about how should you do a console? When you reach out for a console, what should that look like? What questions do you need to ask? What do you need to surface? And part of that includes, what would it look like if I were wrong? Like really looking for disconfirming evidence. It's so important.
turns.zh: 所以我们跟人们聊，你应该怎样去做一次"商量"（consul）。当你伸手去商量时，那应该是什么样子？你需要问哪些问题？你需要把哪些东西摆到台面上？其中一部分还包括：如果我错了，那会是什么样子？就像真的去寻找那些能推翻自己的反面证据（disconfirming evidence）。这太重要了。

turns.en: Why doesn't traditional ethics training work? For all of those reasons, when you think about even maybe the last time you certified, you did an ethics class for your certification, they tend to kind of serve up ethical dilemmas on a platter. Like you know you're getting an ethical dilemma in class, you're right? Well, in real life,
turns.zh: 为什么传统的伦理培训不管用？因为上述所有这些原因。当你想想，哪怕也许是你上一次做认证、上那门伦理课时的情形——它们往往喜欢把伦理困境像端盘子一样端到你面前。就像你知道你在课上就要碰到一个伦理困境了，对吧？可在现实生活里，

turns.en: they don't present themselves like that. Like with some like unclean, unclean leprosy sign in front of them, they just sneak in. If you are not actively asking a question, is there an ethical issue here? And which of us routinely think to ask that? Then it won't even be part of the reasoning. Daniel Cahneman talks about this in the,
turns.zh: 它们并不是那样现身的。它们不会举着"不干净、不干净"的麻风病牌子站在你面前，它们只是悄悄溜进来。如果你不是在主动地问"这里有没有一个伦理问题"——而我们中有谁会例行公事地想到去问这个呢？——那么它甚至都不会成为你推理的一部分。Daniel Kahneman 谈到过这个，

turns.en: he calls it the Y.C. Addy problem. What you see is all there is. So you don't think to ask things like this product provider who's hyping this amazing new product. What aren't they telling me? Who's benefiting from this complexity? Because it's making my eyes cross as I try to read the prospectus. Do I truly understand this?
turns.zh: 他称之为 WYSIATI 问题，也就是"你所看到的就是全部"（what you see is all there is）。所以你想不到去问这样的问题：这个正在吹捧某个了不起的新产品的产品提供商，他们有什么没告诉我？谁在从这种复杂性中获益？因为它复杂得让我读招募说明书（prospectus）时眼睛都花了。我真的理解它吗？

turns.en: Or am I going to tuck and draft behind somebody else's assumed competence and superior knowledge? Those are some of the things that we found that were quite critical. Those were the factors that led people to just kind of go offline. So even if they'd been taught ethical reasoning at some point, it doesn't even get triggered much
turns.zh: 还是我要躲到别人假定的能力和更胜一筹的知识背后去？这些是我们发现的相当关键的一些东西。正是这些因素导致人们干脆"下线"。所以，即便他们曾经在某个时点被教过伦理推理，它也不太会被触发。

turns.en: at a time. You don't even know that you've got an ethical dilemma. You skate across that line because you're too busy. You're incentivized to do so. You're incentivized to look the other way. Well, you don't know what questions to ask. You know, you've done some really good conversations with Jason Pereira over the years.
turns.zh: 在那个当下，你甚至都不知道自己面临一个伦理困境。你就那么从那条线上滑了过去，因为你太忙了。你被激励去这么做。你被激励去把目光移向别处。嗯，你不知道该问什么问题。你知道，这些年来你跟 Jason Pereira 做过一些很棒的对话。

turns.en: He talks about that all the time. Most advisors do not really know how to analyze the quality of any of their offerings. They were not trained in statistics. They don't know how to read the papers. They go to court and they feel prepared to a test to the fact that yes, I was competent to do this.
turns.zh: 他一直在讲这个。大多数顾问其实并不知道如何去评估自己所提供产品的优劣。他们没有受过统计学训练。他们不知道如何去读那些论文。他们上了法庭，感觉自己准备充分，可以证明：是的，我有能力做这件事，

turns.en: And yes, I was acting in the client's best interest and it all falls apart like a house of cards and across examination. Jason has great stories of being an expert witness in those cases and providing the evidence that the advisor did not in fact know what they were doing even if they thought that they did.
turns.zh: 而且是的，我是在为客户的最佳利益行事——结果这一切在交叉盘问（cross examination）下像纸牌屋一样轰然倒塌。Jason 有一些很棒的故事，讲他作为专家证人参与那些案件、提供证据，证明顾问其实并不知道自己在做什么，哪怕他们自以为知道。

turns.en: So that gets us to you better figure out who you want to work for because there are a lot of places that don't have your back. And saying my firm told me to do it is not a defense. Our hearts are particularly heavy for the young people like the one I mentioned at the outset of this call who don't know what they don't know.
turns.zh: 所以这就把我们带到了：你最好搞清楚自己想为谁工作，因为有很多地方是不会在你背后撑你的。而"是我公司让我这么做的"并不是一种抗辩。我们尤其为那些年轻人感到心情沉重，就像我在这通电话开头提到的那位，他们不知道自己不知道什么。

turns.en: There's lots of people giving advice out there who don't even have the basic CFP qualifications or whatever that equivalent is in the UK, Philippa. They might have a particular license to sell a particular thing but they don't know how to look at the overall picture and they don't know how to analyze what they're being told to do.
turns.zh: 外面有很多在提供建议的人，甚至都没有基本的 CFP 资质，或者在英国对应的资质是什么，Philippa。他们也许有一张卖某个特定产品的牌照，但他们不知道如何去看整体图景，也不知道如何去分析别人要他们做的事。

turns.en: I remember the first time that I understood how the RRSP and TFSA accounts work. Those are the registered accounts, the tax preferred accounts that we have in Canada are at least two of them. And it was well after I had been licensed to sell mutual funds and insurance, which is terrifying.
turns.zh: 我记得我第一次真正弄明白 RRSP 和 TFSA 账户是怎么回事的时候——那是我们在加拿大拥有的注册账户、税收优惠账户，至少其中两个是——那已经远在我获准销售共同基金和保险之后了，这想起来很吓人。

turns.en: I remember that light bulb going off and being like, huh, it feels a little bit irresponsible that I was able to sell financial products without understanding this. I've had many similar confessions on the podcast ban over the years. Like it's embarrassing look back at my early years now the industry worked back then totally embarrassing.
turns.zh: 我记得那盏灯泡亮起时的感觉，心想，嘿，我居然能在不理解这些的情况下就卖金融产品，这感觉有点不负责任。这些年来我在播客上听到过很多类似的坦白，比如：现在回头看我早年那样做真难为情，那个年代行业就是这么运转的，太尴尬了。

turns.en: It's ridiculous. And I wish I could say that's in our rear view mirror. But in our book, I kind of take on Canada's banks and some of the undercover investigations that were done very, very recently and the follow-up investigations that were done by the Securities Exchange Commission and what changes as a result of these? Nothing.
turns.zh: 太荒唐了。我真希望能说这已经被我们甩在后视镜里了。但在我们的书里，我算是"开炮"打了加拿大的那些银行，还有最近做的一些卧底调查，以及 Securities Exchange Commission（证券交易委员会）随后做的跟进调查——而这些的结果，改变了什么呢？什么也没有。

turns.en: One third of people who are selling products at banks acknowledge that they don't really know what they're selling or have sold things that are not in the client's best interest. Yikes. On that topic, what role should regulators play in dealing with financial risk conduct? A big one.
turns.zh: 在银行卖产品的人里，有三分之一承认自己其实并不太懂自己在卖什么，或者卖过并不符合客户最佳利益的东西。哎呀。说到这个话题，监管机构在应对金融不当行为方面应该扮演什么角色？一个很大的角色。

turns.en: I come from the UK perspective. It's funny. You see a cycle of a tightening of regulation all sponsored to a scandal usually, right? Yeah, so there's a big scandal. I know, so we had the pension misscelling scandal back in the late 90s. A tightened regulation. Then we had RDR in 2013
turns.zh: 我是从英国的视角来讲。有意思的是，你会看到一个循环：监管的收紧，往往是被一桩丑闻催生出来的，对吧？是的，所以会有一桩大丑闻。我知道，我们在 90 年代末有过养老金误导销售（pension misselling）丑闻，然后监管收紧。接着我们在 2013 年有了 RDR（零售分销审查，Retail Distribution Review），

turns.en: and they did upgrade the requirement for qualifications. So I think joining the financial services profession is not the same as qualifying as a psychiatrist or a psychologist or a lawyer or a doctor. The bar to entry is I think probably too low. But also that tightening of regulation. We're now in the part of the cycle
turns.zh: 他们确实提高了对资质的要求。所以我觉得，进入金融服务业这一行，跟成为一名精神科医生、心理学家、律师或医生并不一样。我认为入门的门槛可能太低了。但同样，那种监管的收紧——我们现在正处在这个循环的另一端：

turns.en: where the government wants gross and so they're looking to dumb down the regulations that isn't in the interest of the general investor who actually probably need something really super dull doesn't need to be invested in individual shares. They need to be in some sort of diversify global portfolio, et cetera, et cetera.
turns.zh: 政府想要增长，于是他们打算把监管"降智"（dumb down）。这并不符合普通投资者的利益。普通投资者其实需要的可能是某种极其无聊的东西，他们并不需要去投个股。他们需要的是某种分散化的全球组合，等等等等。

turns.en: So their role of the regulator, actually, I think, is to fight against that to lobby for tighter regulation and actually to be braver to remove people from the profession itself. I think we don't see enough of that. There's also another part of it for me around what the requirements are for insurance. You can't be qualified advisor
turns.zh: 所以监管机构的作用，我认为，恰恰是去对抗这一点，去游说推动更严格的监管，并且真的要更有勇气把人从这个行业里清除出去。我觉得我们看到的这种事还不够多。对我来说，这里面还有另一部分是关于保险的要求。你不做一名合格顾问，

turns.en: without having the qualifying insurance. Now the detail, if that qualifying insurance, engages the insurers in this question of regulation effectively, because if you can't get insurance, then you can't be regulated. But if we continue to allow insurers to exclude various products or services,
turns.zh: 就拿不到那份合格的保险。如今，那份合格保险的细节，实际上把保险公司也拉进了这个监管问题里——因为如果你拿不到保险，你就没法被监管。可如果我们继续允许保险公司把各种产品或服务排除在外，

turns.en: then they will continue to do that and nothing will change. But actually, they're a really powerful agent for change. If your regulator refuses to allow your insurer to exclude certain liabilities, then you can bet damn sure that those insurers will be all over you because they don't want you to be sued. They don't want you to be fined.
turns.zh: 那他们就会继续这么干，什么也不会改变。但实际上，他们是推动变革的一股非常有力的力量。如果你的监管机构拒绝允许你的保险公司把某些责任排除在外，那你就可以百分百肯定，那些保险公司会死死盯住你——因为他们不想你被起诉，不想你被罚款。

turns.en: There is that side of it as well, which I think is wildly underutilized by regulators globally. Look at the requirements for lawyers in the UK, insurers cannot exclude liability for products or pieces of advice. And therefore, you are at risk of not getting insurance. If you can't get insurance, then you can't trade.
turns.zh: 所以还有这一面，我觉得全球的监管机构都远远没有把它用足。看看英国对律师的要求：保险公司不得把某些产品或某些建议的责任排除在外。因此，你会面临拿不到保险的风险。而如果你拿不到保险，你就没法执业。

turns.en: And it is an extremely powerful thing. We are not using it well enough in the financial services industry, I believe. Really interesting point. Philippa, you mentioned financial problems earlier. What are some other warning signs of possible future misconduct offenders? We talked about early years
turns.zh: 这是一件极其有力的工具。我认为在金融服务业里，我们还没有把它用足。很有意思的观点。Philippa，你前面提到了财务问题。那么，未来可能出现的不当行为者，还有哪些别的危险信号？我们谈到了"早年"（early years），

turns.en: and said the book is written in large parts that early years people as more asserted. They are people who are bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. We talk about Evan in the book, for example, who within a month of qualifying was in the middle of a global fraud. His qualification lasted about nine months and he was in fact banned for life
turns.zh: 并且说这本书很大程度上是写给"早年"人群的，正如你所强调的。他们是那些眼睛发亮、干劲十足的人。我们在书里讲了 Evan 的例子，他获资质不到一个月，就卷入了一场全球性的欺诈。他的资质大约维持了九个月，然后他实际上被英国监管机构

turns.en: by the UK regulator. So early years is a red flag. Being in debt is a red flag. All the vulnerabilities that we talked about earlier being beholden to your boss to pay your mortgage is a problem. Being a people pleaser is something you need to be careful of. Being somebody who is low in self-esteem
turns.zh: 终身禁入。所以"早年"是一个危险信号。负债是一个危险信号。我们前面谈到的所有那些脆弱点——指望老板发薪水来还你的房贷——是个问题。是个爱讨好别人的人，你得小心。是个自尊很低、

turns.en: and therefore wants to buy in self-esteem by buying a Maserati or in certain name of fancy car not massively into cars myself. Somebody who feels the need to keep up with the Joneses, actually. Somebody that hasn't done the work on themselves. Somebody who is tired and just wants the noise to stop.
turns.zh: 因而想靠买一辆 Maserati 或某个牌子的豪车来"买进"自尊的人（我自己对车不太感冒），是个觉得必须跟左邻右舍攀比（keep up with the Joneses）的人，实际上，是个没有在自己身上下过功夫的人，是个累了、只想让噪音停下来的人。

turns.en: There's a whole gamut of really human biases. And that's another reason why we wanted to write this book because I think there's a whole plethora of information out there for the financial services industry about how our clients feel, how our clients behave, what biases affecting your scarce, your tea bias, all that kind of thing.
turns.zh: 这是一整套非常"人性"的偏见。而这也是我们想写这本书的另一个原因，因为我觉得，外面有海量的信息是讲金融服务业的——讲我们的客户有何感受、如何行为，讲哪些偏见在影响着他们，诸如此类。

turns.en: And there's very little out there which focuses on the biases of the advisor themselves. That is part of the reason why this entire book is about where those vulnerabilities might be and gives people that guide path to try and identify where their own personal vulnerabilities might be. There's one of the things we recommend
turns.zh: 而很少有内容是聚焦于顾问自身的那些偏见的。这也是为什么整本书都在讲那些脆弱点可能藏在哪里，并给人们一条指引的路径，去试着识别自己个人的脆弱点可能在哪里。这也是我们推荐的一件事：

turns.en: is that you read this book within a book club so that you can have other people to talk to in a really honest way. I hadn't thought about that. Yeah, I did experience that. And, you know, I love bends that have come in there about, it wasn't until I was so many years qualified, I realized I didn't understand the thing that I was selling.
turns.zh: 就是你在一个读书会（book club）里读这本书，这样你就有其他人可以真诚地交流。这一点我先前没想到过。是啊，我体会过。而且你知道，我很喜欢 Ben 刚才插进来的那段话——直到我执业了这么多年，我才意识到自己并不懂我在卖的东西。

turns.en: And there's a whole plethora but we should recommend that people read this book with other people so that they can do that work together. But the other end of the spectrum from that bright eyed bushy tilt, we highlight a category I've dubbed it the collapsing competent. So this was somebody who might have been very, very good
turns.zh: 诸如此类的坦白多的是。但我们应该建议人们和别人一起读这本书，好让他们能一起做那份功课。而在与那种"眼睛发亮、干劲十足"相对的另一端，我们着重讲了一类人，我给它起了个名字叫"崩塌的能干者"（collapsing competent）。所以这可能是某个曾经非常非常出色、

turns.en: but is being brought down by something and it could be dementia. We've got lots of people working longer in this profession. And if they're ahead of the firm, who's going to tell them? It's like the esop's fable. Who shall bell the cat? I'm not going in there. Are you going in there? That's a real risk factor that
turns.zh: 却正被某种东西拖垮的人，那可能是失智症（dementia）。我们这个行业里有很多人工作时间越来越长。而如果他们是公司的负责人，谁去告诉他们呢？这就像伊索寓言（Aesop's fable）里说的：谁去给猫系铃铛（Who shall bell the cat）？我才不去，你去吗？这是一个真实的风险因素：

turns.en: an impaired brain is not an insightful brain. You are not going to recognize when this stuff is happening to you. You've got to have people around who you can trust to say, I need you to let me know. I remember when my mom said, if you see anything wrong with my driving, you let me know. And when I'm 80, I'm hanging up my keys
turns.zh: 一个受损的大脑不是一个有自知之明的大脑。你不会认出这些东西正在你身上发生。你身边必须有一些你信得过的人，你可以对他们说，我需要你告诉我。我记得我妈妈说过，如果你看到我开车有任何不对劲，你就告诉我。而当我到了 80 岁，我就把钥匙挂起来。

turns.en: and gosh, if she didn't do that proactively. But what do we do for our careers that was that open to feedback? Mostly we're trying to engage in impression management, not tell me the hard stuff. Another one that we took on, this is really a warts and all book, right? Like we dig in and we diagnose in this book
turns.zh: 天哪，她真就那么主动做了。可我们对自己的职业生涯，又何尝这样乐于接受反馈？大多数时候，我们是在忙着做印象管理（impression management），而不是"把难听的话告诉我"。我们涉及的另一个话题——这本书真是一本"warts and all"（不加掩饰、连瑕疵一并呈现）的书，对吧？就像我们在这本书里深挖、我们下诊断，

turns.en: and we don't shy away from addictions, family problems, those are other risk factors that can take people down. You know, when your marriage is falling apart, when your kids are acting in ways that are just horrifying to you, terrifying to you, embarrassing to you, it's really nice to go to work. So nice to go to work.
turns.zh: 而且我们不回避成瘾、家庭问题，那些是能把人拖垮的其他风险因素。你知道，当你的婚姻正在破裂，当你的孩子的行为让你觉得惊恐、恐惧、丢脸时，去上班真是太美好了。去上班太美好了。

turns.en: People like you, they thank you. And work can turn into what's called an applauded addiction. Yay, good for you. Do more. Do more. How about more? And so you end up on this hamster wheel of workaholism because you're really good at it and because you like it often a lot more than you like what's going on at home.
turns.zh: 人们喜欢你，他们谢谢你。而工作可能变成一种所谓的"被喝彩的成瘾"（applauded addiction）：耶，好样的，再多做点，再多做点，再来点怎么样？于是你就踏上了这台"工作狂"的仓鼠跑轮，因为你很擅长它，也因为你往往喜欢它远胜过喜欢家里正在发生的一切。

turns.en: Even the certified fraud examiner study that Philippa alluded to earlier, they do highlight family problems as being present in one in 10 of the cases that they work with. And certainly we know that if somebody's stumbling into work every morning, smelling like they just fell out of the whiskey barrel,
turns.zh: 甚至 Philippa 前面提到的那份 Certified Fraud Examiners（注册舞弊审查师）的研究，他们确实指出，家庭问题出现在他们经手的每 10 个案件中的 1 个里。而我们当然知道，如果某人每天早上跌跌撞撞地来上班、一身像是刚从威士忌桶里爬出来的酒气，

turns.en: you've got to have some way of saying, let me talk, we need to talk. And find out how to get support for people who need it who are struggling. For the retail investors who are listening, I mean, short of smelling someone's a breath to see if they've been drinking or asking if they're having family problems
turns.zh: 你就得有办法说，让我谈谈，我们需要谈谈。并且想办法为那些需要帮助、正在挣扎的人找到支持。对于正在收听的零售投资者（retail investors）来说，我是说，除了去闻某人的口气看他有没有喝酒、或者问他家里有没有家庭问题之外，

turns.en: at home, what can retail investors do to identify high risk advisors before these issues materialize? I always quote a statistic on this. So I was a lawyer for 20 years, sued a lot of finance people a lot. So I've never sued a certified financial planet. Wow. And I have sued a lot of financial people.
turns.zh: 零售投资者能做些什么，去在这些问题浮现之前识别出高风险的顾问呢？我总是引用一个统计数据。所以我做了 20 年律师，起诉过很多金融人士，很多次。而我从来没起诉过一个 CFP（注册理财规划师，certified financial planner）。哇。而我起诉过很多金融人士。

turns.en: That doesn't mean they don't get into regulatory problems but it doesn't tend to be massive. In terms of retail investors being able to identify easily, there isn't a magic silver bullet in any of this stuff. If people have gone to the trouble of certifying themselves, then that is a really good sign.
turns.zh: 这并不意味着他们不会碰到监管麻烦，但那往往不会是那种天大的麻烦。就零售投资者能否轻易识别而言，这里面并没有什么神奇的"银弹"（silver bullet）。如果人们不惜麻烦地去给自己做了认证，那这就是一个非常好的信号。

turns.en: But, you know, I never ran out of work. I had highly intelligent people who were my clients. There really wasn't an easy way to identify the bad guys. Again, that's why we wanted to write this book because we want everyone to do the work on themselves rather than put the obligation on the retail investor.
turns.zh: 但是，你知道，我从来没缺过活儿干。我的客户里有极其聪明的人。真的没有一个简单的办法去识别那些坏人。再说一次，这正是我们想写这本书的原因，因为我们希望每个人都在自己身上下工夫，而不是把责任推给零售投资者。

turns.en: I do think if your advisor's not talking to you about your entire life, then they should be. If they are just talking to you simply about investments and they've never found out about you and your goals and your hopes and your dreams and what you care about and who you are, then that isn't financial planning.
turns.zh: 我确实认为，如果你的顾问不跟你谈你的整个人生，那他就应该谈。如果他们只是单纯地跟你谈投资，从没了解过你、你的目标、你的希望、你的梦想、你在乎什么、你是什么样的人，那就不是财务规划（financial planning）。

turns.en: That is just wealth management. And you need to understand the difference between the two. And I'm not saying wealth managers are the bad guys, not at all, but as a retail investor, you do need to understand the difference between what you could get, what you should get, and what you would get
turns.zh: 那只是财富管理（wealth management）。而你需要理解这两者的区别。我并不是说财富管理人就是坏人，完全不是，但作为一名零售投资者，你确实需要理解：你能得到什么、你应该得到什么，以及如果你去找一个把你当成一个完整的人、

turns.en: if you went to somebody that was looking at you as an entire person, as an entire family, as opposed to a returns first advice process. A couple of weeks ago, we had Barry Reynolds on as a guest. And he said, I think the status correct that he mentioned Ben that 90% of financial products are garbage. Oh, he said crap.
turns.zh: 一个完整的家庭来看待的人，而不是走一个"回报优先"的建议流程，你会得到什么，这三者之间的差别。几周前，我们请了 Barry Reynolds 来做嘉宾。他说，我记得统计没错的话，他跟 Ben 提到，90% 的金融产品都是垃圾。哦，他说的是 crap（烂货）。

turns.en: You can say it, Cameron. I'm just being more plighted in the high road here. But what can advisors do to avoid becoming enamored with bad financial products? They should be as boring as they possibly can be. It is true, isn't it? To be as boring as you possibly can be. And only once you've exhausted the boring, which actually,
turns.zh: 你可以说的，Cameron。我只是在这儿说得婉转点、走正道而已。那么，顾问可以做些什么，来避免自己迷恋上糟糕的金融产品呢？他们应该尽可能地无聊。这是真的，不是吗？要尽可能地无聊。而且只有当你把"无聊"这条路走到头之后——其实，

turns.en: I now run a financial planning firm and we do the most boring investments in advice ever. Most of our clients just don't need anything exciting. So we talk in the book about this complexity here. You know, it feels really special to be part of, only a few people are being offered this particular exciting opportunity.
turns.zh: 我现在经营着一家财务规划公司，我们做的是有史以来最无聊的投资和建议。我们大多数客户根本不需要任何刺激的东西。所以我们在书里谈到了这种"复杂性的诱惑"（complexity here）。你知道，能参与其中、只有少数人被提供这个特别刺激的机会，会让人感觉特别与众不同。

turns.en: And in the same way as the back follows the money, it is your obligation to understand exactly how this works. And if it doesn't, if you don't understand it, even if it's the best thing ever, you should not be advising on it. It is literally your job to understand exactly where that money is going, how it is making a return,
turns.zh: 而就像"跟着钱走"（follow the money）一样，你有责任去弄明白这到底是怎么运作的。而如果你弄不明白，如果你不理解它，那么哪怕它是史上最好的东西，你也不该去给它做建议。搞清楚那笔钱到底流向哪里、它是怎么产生回报的，

turns.en: making sure that that makes sense in your mind as to why that's making a return. If you've got cross jurisdictional stuff, then why on earth are you looking across your jurisdictional stuff? Who is that benefiting? If you have multiple layers of fees, who's getting paid why they're getting paid? Why do you need multiple levels of fees?
turns.zh: 字面上就是你的工作，你要在心里确信它为什么会产生回报。如果你有跨司法辖区（cross jurisdictional）的东西，那你到底为什么要去看跨司法辖区的东西？那对谁有利？如果你有多层费用（multiple layers of fees），谁在拿钱、为什么拿钱？你为什么需要多层费用？

turns.en: Why doesn't need to be this complicated? If you have cross currency, why on earth have you got cross currency stuff in there? There's another red flag and another complexity risk. You should be looking at this, asking questions and being the most annoying person that you possibly can because your role is not to sell products.
turns.zh: 为什么它非得这么复杂？如果你有跨币种（cross currency）的东西，那你到底为什么要在里面放跨币种的东西？那又是一个危险信号，又一重复杂性风险。你应该审视这些，去提问，做那个你能做到的最"招人烦"的人，因为你的角色不是卖产品。

turns.en: Your role isn't to impress the person that comes to you with that product. Your absolute responsibility is to act in the best interests of your client. And if you wouldn't sell it to your family, why on earth are you considering selling it to any of your clients? Oh, sing it sister. I just saw too much of this.
turns.zh: 你的角色不是去给那个拿着产品来找你的人留下深刻印象。你绝对的责任，是为你客户的最佳利益行事。而如果一样东西你不会卖给自己的家人，那你到底为什么还在考虑把它卖给你的任何一个客户呢？哦，说得好，姐妹。我见过太多这样的事了。

turns.en: Based on all of my career was based around stuff that the advisors didn't really understand. And then they didn't understand the downside. And they couldn't talk about the downside and they couldn't anticipate the downside. And when the downside happened, they said, oh, well, nobody forced all that was an awful.
turns.zh: 我整个职业生涯都是围绕着那些顾问其实并不真正理解的东西展开的。然后他们不理解下行风险。他们没法谈论下行风险，也没能预见到下行风险。而当下行风险真的发生时，他们就说，哦，嗯，没人逼你，那太糟糕了，

turns.en: It was your fault because you were too greedy client. And so I was doing my best. I gave you this great product. And it's just not my problem or my fault. We are on the same page on investments. Should be very boring. You said you don't think your clients need the more complex stuff. I don't think most people need the more complex stuff
turns.zh: 那是你的错，因为你太贪心了，客户。所以呢，我可是尽了全力，我给了你这个很棒的产品，这就不是我的问题、也不是我的错了。我们在投资这件事上是站在同一边的：投资应该非常无聊。你说你觉得你的客户不需要那些更复杂的东西。我觉得大多数人都不需要那些更复杂的东西，

turns.en: to get sold to more people than it should be sold to. I'm curious, Phillipa, in all the cases that you've seen, you talked about how there wasn't an obvious way to identify the people doing this conduct before the fact. Do you think there's a relationship though between the financial literacy of the victims
turns.zh: 可它却被卖给了远超过应该买它的人数。我很好奇，Philippa，在你见过的所有案子里，你谈到事前并没有什么明显的办法去识别那些做出这种行为的人。那你觉得，受害者的金融素养（financial literacy）和他们成为受害者的倾向之间，有没有某种关系呢？

turns.en: and their propensity to be victimized? I saw really interesting questions. So I acted for anyone from calm mechanics to teachers, to hedge fund managers, to doctors, to the whole gamut of financially sophisticated to financially unsophisticated. I acted for over a thousand British steel steel workers
turns.zh: 这是个非常有意思的问题。所以我代理过的客户，从普通机修工到老师，到对冲基金经理，到医生，覆盖了从财务上很老练到财务上很不老练的整个光谱。我代理过超过一千名 British Steel 的钢铁工人，

turns.en: who were very much not financially sophisticated. And I don't mean that in any rude way. They simply weren't. But frankly, who is sophisticated? To the extent that you might need to be to second guess a complex product? Who really, who's not in the financial services industry and advising on it, understands how pensions work?
turns.zh: 他们在财务上非常不老练。我说这话没有任何不敬的意思。他们就是不老练而已。但坦白讲，谁才算老练呢？老练到足以去识破一个复杂产品的程度？除了金融服务业里那些真正在给它做建议的人之外，谁真的懂养老金（pensions）是怎么运作的？

turns.en: I actually don't think that there is a direct correlation between financial sophistication and getting caught up in this stuff. It is far more emotional than anything else. So when I talk about the steel workers who were transferred out of their final salary pension scheme, that was all emotional.
turns.zh: 我其实不认为金融素养和卷入这种事情之间有直接的相关性。这件事里，情绪的成分远大于其他任何东西。所以当我讲那些被从"最终薪资"（final salary）养老金计划里转出来的钢铁工人时，那全都是情绪驱动的。

turns.en: But you don't want Tata to have your money. You want that to go to your family, don't you? When you die? So it was all emotional decisions and this kind of white coat relationship. You know better than me. The regulator has authorized you. Therefore you have a tick in that box. Therefore I should trust you. You know what to do.
turns.zh: "你不想让 Tata 拿着你的钱，你想让那笔钱在你死后留给你的家人，不是吗？"所以那全都是情绪化的决定，加上这种"白大褂"式的关系：你比我懂，监管机构授权了你，所以那个框里打了个勾，所以我应该信任你，你知道该怎么做。

turns.en: And actually it's kind of too difficult. I'm too busy doing my stuff. I want to delegate this. I want somebody else to have responsibility for it. Let's go for it. And as I said earlier, I cannot tell you how many of my clients said to me, I never asked the question. I'll curious why, what your experiences in similar situations?
turns.zh: 而且实际上这也太难了。我太忙着自己的事了。我想把这个委托出去。我想让别人来为此负责。那就上吧。而且就像我前面说的，我数不清有多少客户对我说过，我从没问过那个问题。我很好奇为什么，你在类似情形下的经历是怎样的？

turns.en: I think it's really hard for us to deal with competing experts. I can remember just under podcast with Robin Powell in the UK who's very much into sort of the boring investments. I talked to him about some financial advice that we were being given as a family and all of the counterpoints that that advisor was giving
turns.zh: 我觉得，对我们来说，很难去应对"相互打架的专家"（competing experts）。我记得就在不久前，我和英国的 Robin Powell 一起做了一期播客，他非常热衷于那种"无聊的投资"。我跟他聊了我们作为一个家庭当时正在接受的一些理财建议，以及那位顾问给出的所有反驳点，

turns.en: for why the boring investments weren't good. And he just went, oh my. I understand why it's hard to stand in the presence of somebody who's telling you why this time it's different. Why this particular complexity of product is important for you and your family to have. And I will be behind you to make sure
turns.zh: 说为什么那些无聊的投资不好。他就"哦，天哪"了一声。我明白，为什么站在那个正告诉你"这次不一样"、"这个特别复杂的产品对你和你的家庭很重要"、"我会守在你们身后、确保我们在需要退出时恰好在最合适的时机退出"的人面前，很难顶得住。我又懂什么呢？

turns.en: that we get out at just the right time if we need to get out. What do I know? What I know now is I have probably 7,000 more hours of statistics training than that guy ever had. But I didn't have a designation and I wasn't in that role. And mostly we get just tired and we want somebody to take care of our stuff
turns.zh: 我现在懂的是，我大概比那家伙多受过 7000 个小时的统计学训练。但我当时没有一个头衔，也不在那个角色里。而且大多数时候，我们只是累了，我们想让别人来照看我们不想照看的东西。

turns.en: that we don't want to take care of. Somebody is saying that we could do better. And that would make a difference in our life. Those are very compelling words. They don't necessarily activate greed. They activate a sense of responsibility. That you should do this thing. I think as just regular consumers, research, research,
turns.zh: 有人说我们能做得更好，说那会给我们的生活带来改变。那些是非常有说服力的话。它们激活的不一定是贪婪。它们激活的是一种责任感：你应该做这件事。我想，作为普通的消费者，就是研究、研究、

turns.en: research, you can find out if your CFP has any regulatory strikes against him or her. That's publicly available knowledge. You can find out who is this person behind the desk at the bank giving you advice and what allows them to be qualified. The challenge as we know now, then in caremen is that it's often hard
turns.zh: 再研究。你可以查出你的 CFP 有没有任何监管方面的"污点"（regulatory strikes）。那是公开可查的信息。你可以查出银行桌子后面那个给你建议的人是谁，是什么让他们有资格。而难题在于——我们现在、以及在 Kahneman 那里都知道——对于那些没有很多钱的人来说，

turns.en: for people who don't have huge amounts of money to get neutral, good, high quality advice. Because they gravitate towards product providers that are incentivized to sell them the products that they have that they own. So that's an issue. We asked one question earlier about what would be some warning signs.
turns.zh: 往往很难获得中立、优质、高质量的建议。因为他们会向那些产品提供商靠拢，而那些提供商是被激励去把自己拥有、自己在卖的产品卖给他们的。所以那是个问题。我们前面问过一个关于"危险信号"的问题。

turns.en: This isn't necessarily for the investor, the consumer. But one of the things that you need to know as a manager is that if your team, which was previously coherent and cohesive and they all seem to be getting along, is suddenly there's weird stuff going on. You're sensing alliances, you're sensing discontent.
turns.zh: 这不一定是对投资者、消费者而言的。但作为一名管理者，你需要知道的一点是：如果你的团队原本 coherent（协调一致）、cohesive（凝聚力强），大家看起来相处融洽，却突然出现了一些古怪的事——你感觉到有派系结盟，你感觉到有不满情绪，

turns.en: Somebody might be reporting bullying or intimidation. That is a really, really good sign that you have a fox in the hen house that a psychopath has entered the mix where one of these snakes and suits, you need to investigate because they always cause difficulties in team functioning. So if that's going on as a manager, take note.
turns.zh: 有人可能在报告霸凌或恐吓——那就是一个非常非常好的迹象，说明你的鸡舍里混进了一只狐狸（a fox in the hen house），一个精神变态者进入了这个组合，或者其中一条"西装革履的毒蛇"进来了。你需要去调查，因为他们总是会给团队运作制造麻烦。所以，如果这种情况正在发生，作为管理者，要留意。

turns.en: That's a huge red flag. Each of you came into this project with such unique experiences and backgrounds at tremendous amount of experience, relevant experience to this topic. But what do you think your biggest learnings were from writing this book? I know, so I could answer that. I would need another hour.
turns.zh: 那是一个巨大的危险信号。你们每一位都带着如此独特的经历和背景来到这个项目，拥有与这个话题高度相关的大量经验。那么，你们觉得写这本书最大的收获是什么？我知道，所以我可以回答这个。我可能需要再一个小时。

turns.en: There is the importance of relationships within and without the firm, the importance of knowing myself and doing the work on myself, the importance of understanding, we are all vulnerable and one thing that we were really aware of as we went through the book was ensuring that people didn't read the book and say, well, that's okay
turns.zh: 有公司内外关系的重要性，有了解我自己、在自己身上下工夫的重要性，有理解"我们全都是脆弱的"这一事实的重要性。而我们在写这本书的过程中非常在意的一件事，就是要确保人们读完之后不会说，嗯，那没关系，

turns.en: because I would never do that. And I did this through writing this with Moira is to understand where my own personal vulnerabilities are and that we are all incredibly delightfully and wonderfully human. And that being kind to yourself is a super important part of your ethical health.
turns.zh: 因为我绝不会做那种事。而我通过与 Moira 一起写这本书所做到的，就是去理解我自己个人的脆弱点在哪里，以及我们所有人都是极其"可爱地、美妙地"人性十足的。而对自己友善，是你的"伦理健康"里超级重要的一部分。

turns.en: One of the big learnings for me was about something called the illusion of superiority or the better than average effect, which is the notion that we often rank ourselves as being better drivers, better health nuts, whatever. We see ourselves as being higher than average on a number of dimensions,
turns.zh: 对我来说，最大的收获之一是关于一个叫做"优越感错觉"（illusion of superiority）或"优于平均效应"（better than average effect）的东西，也就是这样一个观念：我们常常把自己排在"更好的司机、更注重健康的人"等等之列。我们在很多维度上都把自己看得高于平均水平，

turns.en: which, you know, you can just sort of laugh at, but there's one domain without illusion is on steroids and that is within the domain of morality. None of us want to contemplate the fact that we might just be normally ethical, average ethical. Of course, they're better than that. But the moral humility is something that the regulators,
turns.zh: 这你知道，你尽可以一笑置之。但有一个领域，这种错觉简直像打了类固醇一样夸张，那就是道德这个领域。我们中没有一个人愿意去设想这样一个事实：我们也许只是道德上"正常"、"平均水平"而已。"我当然比那强。"但那种道德上的谦逊（moral humility），是当监管机构——

turns.en: when we came back and we asked all of the people who we interviewed for the book, including you, Cam, about how should one stay ethical, almost to a person, everybody said, some version of their, but for the grace of God, go, I, it could have been me and I'm just really lucky that life circumstances and the supports around me
turns.zh: 当我们回过头去、问所有我们为这本书采访过的人，包括你，Cam，一个人应该如何保持有道德时——几乎每一个人，都说了某种版本的"若非上帝恩典，那个人就是我"（there but for the grace of God go I）：那本可能就是我，而我只是非常幸运，人生的际遇和我身边的支持

turns.en: have helped keep me upright. Moral humility is something to be cultivated, to be welcomed. The second big learning for me is that we have to learn to tolerate being uncomfortable and to not treat it like it's a nuisance, but to treat that discomfort as meaningful data that we need to pause and name and explore.
turns.zh: 帮我一直站得笔直。道德上的谦逊，是一种值得培养、值得欢迎的品质。对我来说，第二个大收获是：我们必须学会忍受不适，不去把它当成一种讨厌的干扰，而是把那种不适当作有意义的数据——我们需要停下来，为它命名，去探索它。

turns.en: And then the third learning for me was unequivocally, navigate your way to good employment. If you have any sense that something in your firm is wiffy, get out of there. It will shape you in ways that you won't like and it will not protect you if the regulators come calling. So find good people to work for, create your own firm
turns.zh: 然后第三个收获对我来说是毫不含糊的：给自己导航到一份好的雇佣关系里去。如果你有任何一点感觉，觉得你公司里有什么东西"气味不对"（wiffy），就离开那里。它会以你不喜欢的方式塑造你，而且当监管机构上门时，它不会保护你。所以去找好的人为之工作，如果非得如此，总有一天去创立你自己的公司，

turns.en: someday if that's what it takes, but navigate your way, get the best qualifications that you possibly can for the position that you're interested in, volunteer, network, find people, and keep yourself financially free. Don't let yourself become overextended. Of course, everybody in society is dependent
turns.zh: 但你要为自己导航，为你感兴趣的职位拿到你能拿到的最好资质，去做志愿者，去建立人脉，去找人，并且让自己在财务上保持自由。别让自己过度负债（overextended）。当然，社会里的每个人都指着

turns.en: on their employer to pay their mortgage, but work your way up to having some degree of choice over these matters. Our final question, how do you reach to find success in your lives? I knew you were going to ask this question because I've listened to your podcast. It was a really interesting thought process
turns.zh: 雇主来还房贷，但你要一步步往上走，直到在这些事情上拥有某种程度的选择权。我们最后一个问题：你们如何在自己的人生中定义成功（reach to find success）？我就知道你会问这个问题，因为我听过你们的播客。这是个非常有意思的思考过程，

turns.en: as I went through this and I was walking along, mulling it over because thinking walks are really good. And the conclusion I came to was, I'm living it. I am, this is success. I have a job that fulfills me that is congruent with my values. That feels amazing. I can push things forward.
turns.zh: 因为我一路走、一路琢磨这件事——因为边走路边思考是很好的。而我得出的结论是：我正在过着它。我就是在过，这就是成功。我有一份让我有成就感、与我的价值观相符的工作。那感觉棒极了。我能推动事情向前。

turns.en: We held a big event the other day about climate change. I can go out there and I can make that happen. That's amazing. I get to have written this amazing book with this amazing woman and ask this deep, deep question that we spend, I think, two and a half years almost three years contemplating and talking to people. I have amazing friends.
turns.zh: 前几天我们办了一场关于气候变化（climate change）的大型活动。我能走到台前去，把那样的事办成。这太棒了。我得以和这位了不起的女性一起写出这本了不起的书，去追问这个深深的、深深的问题——我们花了差不多两年半、将近三年的时间去沉思、去和人交谈。我有很棒的朋友。

turns.en: I have amazing family. I have enough money. I don't lust after the miserities of this world. I get to go on holiday. I don't have to add up food as I go around the supermarket. I can give and I do time and money. I am basically living my version of success. And thank you for asking that question
turns.zh: 我有很棒的家庭。我有足够的钱。我并不垂涎这世上的浮华虚荣。我能去度假。我在超市里走的时候，不必一边逛一边把账加起来。我能够给予，而且我确实付出了时间和金钱。我基本上正过着我自己版本的成功。而谢谢你问这个问题，

turns.en: because it allowed me to say, I'm living it. I am successful. And that feels absolutely amazing. Why not? You know, it depends on the day. Some days, success feels like I remembered that password. Finally. But on a more global perspective that Philip was taking, it has so much to do with having some measure of control.
turns.zh: 因为它让我得以说出：我正在过着它。我是成功的。而那感觉绝对棒极了。为什么不呢？你知道，这要看是哪一天。有些日子，成功的感觉就像"我终于想起那个密码了"。但从一个更宏观的角度看——也就是 Philippa 所持的那个角度——它跟"拥有某种程度的掌控"关系极大，

turns.en: I'm aware of or freedom to choose. And I'm aware of just how much privilege I have in being able to choose some of the things and that in turn choosing the right things opens you up to having more freedom to make good choices. But for me, it comes down to things like relationships over achievement, wholeness over accumulation.
turns.zh: 或者说，是选择的自由。而我也清楚，能够选择其中一些事情，我享有多大的特权；反过来，选择对的事情，又会为你打开更多做出好选择的自由。但对我来说，它归结为这样一些东西：关系高于成就，完整（wholeness）高于积累（accumulation）。

turns.en: I really want to be a safe harbor and a force for good in this world. I want to not disappoint the people that matter to me, my family, my children, my friends, not that momentary disappointment of no, But I want to be somebody that they are proud to have known or to be related to that alignment between values and action under pressure.
turns.zh: 我真的很想成为这个世界上的一个"安全港"（safe harbor）、一股向善的力量。我不想让那些对我重要的人失望——我的家人、我的孩子、我的朋友——不是那种"不行"的一时失望，而是我想成为一个他们会以认识、或以之为亲为荣的人。那种在压力之下价值观与行动之间的契合，

turns.en: And the things that could be true of you no matter where you fall on the socio-economic spectrum, those markers of integrity are what really stand out to me now. Can I ask you to a question if that's all right? Sure. What stood out from the book to you to you when you read it? The biggest thing for me was just the concept
turns.zh: 以及那些无论你落在社会经济光谱的哪个位置都可能成立的品质——那些正直（integrity）的标志——才是如今真正让我看重的东西。我能问你一个问题吗，如果可以的话？当然。你读这本书时，最让你印象深刻的是什么？对我来说最大的一点，就是那个概念——

turns.en: of behavioral ethics, which I think is a big part of what the book ends up being about. I think this idea that we can have a rational ethical framework and people can know what they should do and they can know right from wrong. But for various reasons, they can still end up doing bad things.
turns.zh: 行为伦理学（behavioral ethics），我认为它是这本书最终在很大程度上讲的东西。我觉得这个理念是：我们可以有一个理性的伦理框架，人们可以知道自己该怎么做，可以知道什么是对、什么是错，但由于种种原因，他们仍然可能最后做了坏事。

turns.en: As we talked about earlier, you need to have culture, you need to have systems in place, you need to check in with yourself and be very in tune with yourself to understand where your vulnerabilities are. But just that concept of just like with other parts of life, we can have rational frameworks for things
turns.zh: 正如我们前面谈到的，你需要有文化，你需要有到位的系统，你需要跟自己"签到"、跟自己非常合拍，去理解你的脆弱点在哪里。但正是这个概念——就像生活的其他部分一样，我们可以为事情建立理性的框架，

turns.en: and we can say what people should do in certain situations. But that's often going to be very different from what they will actually do and understanding where those vulnerabilities are is really, I would argue more important to acting ethically than understanding right from wrong. I actually sent myself a picture
turns.zh: 我们可以说在某些情形下人们应该怎么做——但那往往跟他们实际会做的非常不同。而理解那些脆弱点在哪里，我认为，比理解什么是对什么是错，对于做出合伦理的行为更重要。我其实给自己发了一张图片，

turns.en: to a screenshot of the moral operating system. I could tell you put a lot of work into that, at least I believe you did, and just to go through that wheel, now you have to spend a little bit of time with it, but it's such a thought-provoking each one of the pieces of pies on that wheel is pretty clear and can really cause someone to think
turns.zh: 是那个道德操作系统（moral operating system）的一张截图。我看得出来你在上面下了很多功夫，至少我相信你下了。就去走一遍那个轮盘——你得在上面花点时间——但它太能引人深思了。那个轮盘上的每一块"饼"都相当清晰，真的能促使一个人去思考，

turns.en: and it's worthwhile time to be spent. So I thought that was really nice to kind of encapsulate everything that was in the book, especially being in the industry. It's an interesting read and it's an easy read. Secudo is a both on this great accomplishment. This was an enormous amount of work clearly.
turns.zh: 那份时间是值得花的。所以我觉得，把书里的一切这样浓缩起来，真的很棒，尤其是身处这个行业里。它是一本有意思、也读起来轻松的书。恭喜你们俩取得这项了不起的成就。这显然是极其庞大的工作量。

turns.en: Thank you for noting the behavioral ethics part of it, and I think that that's been the part that's been missing for me within all of the financial ethics training is where are people in this? Obviously I have a bias to that as a psychologist, but the regulators begged us to help people understand it.
turns.zh: 谢谢你指出其中"行为伦理学"那一部分，我认为那正是我在所有金融伦理培训里一直觉得缺失的部分——人们在这一切里究竟处在什么位置。显然，作为一名心理学家，我对此有偏见，但监管机构恳求我们去帮助人们理解这一点。

turns.en: It's their humanity that needs to come into play and that includes their own biases and things that you can't just will yourself out of, you need to learn how to work with them. I love the fact that you're going to go and do the moral operating system work. We wanted to give people something actionable to take away
turns.zh: 正是他们的人性需要被纳入考量，而这其中包括他们自己的偏见，包括那些你没法靠意志就摆脱掉的东西——你得学会如何与它们共处。我很喜欢你打算去做那套道德操作系统功课这件事。我们想给人们一些可以带走的、可操作的东西，

turns.en: because that behavioral ethics piece does need that. And your advice to read this as a study group? I think that's wise council. Yeah, and we would love to hear from people as and when they do. I mean, we've sent this book out into the world. Our greatest hope is that it actually makes a difference.
turns.zh: 因为"行为伦理学"那一部分确实需要这个。还有你们那条"把这本书当成一个学习小组来读"的建议？我觉得那是明智的忠告。是啊，我们也很想听听大家读完之后的反馈。我是说，我们已经把这本书送进了这个世界。我们最大的希望，是它真的能带来一点改变。

turns.en: And I think we said the other day we will have failed. If it's made no difference to the world that's what we want. So we would really genuinely love to hear from people as they run through the book and please do ask his questions. Terrific. Well, Philip, great to meet you, Moira, your long-term friends are great to see you again.
